nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug

First of all, thank you so much for taking the time to review this report. We truly appreciate all your work.

Let's say I have two arrays X and Y with the shapes X.shape = (10, u, v) and Y.shape = (20, u, v)
The first 10 rows of X and Y are exactly the same. In other words, you can pass the assert torch.all(X == Y[:10]) assertion.
Now, you evaluate torch.sum on the last two dimensions.

X_sum = torch.sum(X, dim=(1,2))
Y_sum = torch.sum(Y, dim=(1,2))


Since X and Y[:10] are exactly the same, you would expect that X_sum and Y_sum[:10] should also be exactly the same. However, my example shows that there can be a slight mismatch.

To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Please download the input data numpy file sum_bug_data.npz from Box and place it somewhere on your disk.

I'm sorry that the file is huge (i.e., 60 MB), but this is the smallest file I could generate to produce such an issue.


Open a python terminal in the same folder.
Run the following script:

import numpy as np
import torch
npz_file = np.load('sum_bug_data.npz')
A, B = npz_file['A'], npz_file['B']

X_np = A
Y_np = np.concatenate([A, B], axis=0)
X = torch.from_numpy(X_np).cuda()
Y = torch.from_numpy(Y_np).cuda()

assert A.shape == (10, 7923, 100)
assert B.shape == (10, 7923, 100)
assert X.shape == (10, 7923, 100)
assert Y.shape == (20, 7923, 100)

X_sum = torch.sum(X, dim=(1,2)) 
Y_sum = torch.sum(Y, dim=(1,2)) 
print('X     ==     Y[:10] -> ', torch.all(X     ==     Y[:10]))
print('X_sum == Y_sum[:10] -> ', torch.all(X_sum == Y_sum[:10]))
print('-'*80)
with np.printoptions(precision=10):
    print('X_sum[:10] ->\n', X_sum[:10].detach().cpu().numpy().reshape(-1))
    print('Y_sum[:10] ->\n', Y_sum[:10].detach().cpu().numpy().reshape(-1))
    print('-'*80)
    print('X_sum[:10] == Y_sum[:10] ->\n', (X_sum[:10] == Y_sum[:10]))


Expected behavior
Since X and Y[:10] are exactly the same, you would expect that X_sum and Y_sum[:10] should also be exactly the same. However, my example shows that there can be a slight mismatch.  In particular, there is a slight mismatch in the elements 1.7900770e+32 and 1.7900768e+32.

🐛 Critical bug
If a PyTorch release is built with a compiler that doesn't support all the AVX512 intrinsics in the codebase, then it won't have ATen AVX512 kernels, but at runtime, CPU capability would still be incorrectly returned as AVX512 on a machine that supports AVX512. It seems that PyTorch Linux releases are done on CentOS with gcc 7.3, so this bug would manifest in the 1.10 release, unless fixed. gcc versions below 9.0 don't support all the AVX512 intrinsics in the codebase, such as _mm512_set_epi8.
PyTorch nightly releases also seem to have this issue.
I'm sorry for having introduced this bug. 😞
To Reproduce

Build from source with a compiler that doesn't support all the AVX512 intrinsics used in the codebase.
gcc versions below 9 can be used to reproduce the issue on a machine that supports AVX512.
ATen AVX512 kernels won't be compiled.
Open a Python interpreter. Use print(torch.__config__.show())
CPU Capability would be displayed as AVX512.


Expected behavior
If a binary is built with a compiler that doesn't support all the necessary AVX512 intrinsics, then it shouldn't report CPU Capability as AVX512 on a machine that supports all the required AVX512 instruction sets.

Environment
PyTorch Builder seems to be using CentOS with gcc 7.3 for releases, so nightly releases are being built without AVX512 support in ATen, but CPU Capability is still being displayed as AVX512 in print(torch.__config__.show()) .

PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0):
Nightly releases

Fix
There are two parts to this issue -

To ensure that users are not misled, CPU Capability should be returned as AVX512 at runtime only if the binary was built with a compiler that supports all the AVX512 intrinsics in the codebase. I opened #66703 for it.
To ensure that AVX512 ATen kernels are included in the release binaries, can gcc version 9 or above be used instead in PyTorch Builder? Thanks!

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @jbschlosser @seemethere @malfet @pytorch/pytorch-dev-infra

🚀 Feature

Add inverse function for torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_sequence that takes PackedSequence object as input and returns list of variable length Tensors.
Motivation

Working with sequential data with variable length (e.g. working with text or time series using LSTM) the proposed function is almost always needed but you have to implement it yourself.
Pitch

n/a
Alternatives

n/a
Additional context

Usage example (link):
import torch
from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pack_sequence, pad_packed_sequence


def unpack_sequence(packed_sequences):
    """Unpacks PackedSequence into a list of variable length Tensors"""
    
    unpacked_sequences = []
    
    padded_sequences, lengths = pad_packed_sequence(packed_sequences, batch_first=True)
    
    max_length = padded_sequences.shape[1]
    idx = torch.arange(max_length)

    for seq, length in zip(padded_sequences, lengths):
        mask = idx < length
        unpacked_seq = seq[mask]
        unpacked_sequences.append(unpacked_seq)
        
    return unpacked_sequences


a = torch.tensor([1,2,3])
b = torch.tensor([4,5])
c = torch.tensor([6])

sequences = [a, b, c]
packed_sequences = pack_sequence(sequences)
unpacked_sequences = unpack_sequence(packed_sequences)

assert all([torch.allclose(a, b) for a, b in zip(sequences, unpacked_sequences)])

To Reproduce
After split my model, there is the sample which will rise the error:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class Test(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.T = nn.Parameter(torch.eye(512))
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, 2, 1)
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(True)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.inverse(self.T).matmul(x)
        out = self.conv(x)
        out = self.bn(out)
        out = self.relu(out)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(torch.__version__)

    model = Test().eval()

    x = torch.randn((1, 3, 512, 512))
    out = model(x)

    # TorchScript
    model_jit = torch.jit.trace(model, (x))
    model_jit.save("model_jit.pt")
    print(model_jit.code)

    # Optimize
    from torch.utils.mobile_optimizer import optimize_for_mobile
    model_jit_opt = optimize_for_mobile(model_jit)
    model_jit_opt.save("model_jit_opt.pth")
    print(model_jit_opt.code)

    model_jit_opt = model_jit_opt.eval()

    # export to Onnx
    torch.onnx.export(model_jit_opt,
        (x),

Here is the question: given Tensor[] or Tensor?[] in JIT schema, what C++ type should a kernel implementing this function take?
Historically, we have two divergent answers for Tensor[] case:

The unboxed C++ API says you get a TensorList aka ArrayRef<Tensor>, which is essentially a contiguous array of Tensors
The boxed API says you get c10::List<Tensor>, which is a refcounted pointer to an array of IValues (which happen to be Tensors)

There doesn't seem to be a single correct representation. The boxed representation is heinously inefficient (requiring a dynamic allocation for the array, and requiring ownership of all the tensors), but it has uniform representation and thus works with the JIT interpreter. The unboxed representation is good for direct C++ API calls (as it is compatible with initializer_list) but sometimes it is not very convenient; for example, if you have two const Tensor&, the only way to assemble them into a TensorList is to do a refcount bump at the new location (unless you play tricks like TensorRef--see OptionalTensorRef), similarly, if you have an ArrayRef, this is not convertible to ArrayRef<optional> without doing a dynamic allocation for the conversion. In an ideal world, we'd be able to support all these use cases:

C++ API initializer list call {x, y}
C++ API call with ArrayRef
C++ API call with ArrayRef
Boxed call with IValue (internally containing c10::List)
For optional, also:

C++ API call with ArrayRef<optional<Tensor{,Ref}>>
C++ API call with ArrayRef<Tensor{,Ref}> but where undefined tensors represent missing tensors
Boxed call with IValue (internally containing c10::List)



Without:

Forcing refcount bumps
Forcing an O(n) copy of the data structure to an alternate representation (no dynamic allocations)
Efficient access from within the kernel

Well, you know what they say: if you can't pick one, pick 'em all. Let's make a ITensorList type which internally is a union over all of the representations we care about. As a start, this would be ArrayRef<Tensor> (the current cpp/dispatcher API type) and c10::List<Tensor>* (the boxed representation; this had better be a non-owning reference, BTW!) ITensorList would do an if-statement over the representation type and call the appropriate accessor logic depending on what it actually holds. It probably doesn't need to support too many APIs; just iteration and indexing.
The point is that the union is extensible over future types; if we ever have another type that would have required a conversion, we can instead add it directly to the union. The conversions then only happen when we read out the tensors, but since we read them individually, and as const references we have managed to eliminate the cost of allocating another intermediate data structure. The cost of this is the condition branch on access, but you should only really be iterating through the list once anyway.
Flipping the representation everywhere may be a bit painful, but we can put this in place for structured kernels and incrementally port in this way.
Once this is done, there are a lot of follow ups:

Change dispatcher API to use this type
Modify boxed-unboxed template to use this logic to avoid intermediate conversion
Change C++ API to allow passing other types (like c10::List) by generating extra overloads. We could also perhaps make the C++ API directly accept ITensorList if this doesn't cause ambiguity (you'll need a lot of implicit constructors)
Do this all again for list of optional tensors, with the added complication of punning undefined tensor and nullopt tensor. Also note that currently C++ API takes c10::List<optional<Tensor>> so we definitely want to bring back ArrayRef<Tensor> as a valid spelling in C++ API
Maybe do this again for ArrayRef? (Which gets stored as c10::List in boxed world?) Note that actually ArrayRef is a pretty good API on the kernel end when the size of the integer array is statically known or bounded because you can allocate the read out on the stack, but unfortunately we still allocate a full vector in those cases

See also #54058
